title: UBS picks 11 potential AI winners
full_text:
The AI revolution ain't coming, it's already here. If Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's big speech on artificial intelligence wasn't proof enough, then a new deep dive into Australia's artificial intelligence opportunity compiled by UBS strategist Richard Schellbach and economist George Tharenou confirms it.
It starts with a stunning figure: the value of data centres under construction in Australia, which already stands at $21.6 billion, could double over the next 18 months towards a peak that is equivalent to 2 per cent of gross domestic product.
It's a reminder that, whether AI works or not, whether this is a bubble or not, we are now firmly in the grip of "the most significant investment cycle since the mining boom". It won't reach those heights - the mining boom peaked at 7 per cent of GDP, and created tens of thousands more jobs than the data centre boom will - but the impact on the economy is real, and growing.
For example, Tharenou expects the lift in demand created by the data centre boom - for material, for land, for labour - will prove impervious to rising interest rates and inflationary pressures, adding to the case for the RBA to raise rates.
Only over the longer term, Tharenou expects AI-related investment to "eventually improve productivity, and then become somewhat disinflationary".
The question of how AI will hit jobs is also ever-present. Although a report on AI and employment, released last week by the federal Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, found "no evidence to date of broad labour market upheaval driven by AI", estimates across UBS' analyst team suggest the pain may be coming over the next three to five years.
UBS sees the potential for ASX companies to shed between 10 per cent and 15 per cent of their workforces under a moderate AI adoption scenario, and almost 20 per cent under a more extreme scenario.
Clearly, those estimates need to be taken with a grain of salt. But we'd suggest there would be few economists or Treasury officials who have anything like those sorts of job losses in their long-term models.
AI's effects on equity markets are already visible. Schellbach notes that equity capital market volumes have been dominated by AI-related activity this year. Companies connected to the thematic have raised almost double the amount raised by the mining sector - despite the tech sector accounting for a very small percentage of the ASX's total market capitalisation.
Similarly, the threat of AI disruption has cut a swath through sectors such as software and other industries considered capital-lite. UBS' basket of ASX stocks with high levels of intangible assets is down 35 per cent over the past year.
Five questions point to winners and losers
These bigger-picture shifts are arguably well recognised. What investors are obsessing over is which stocks will emerge as AI winners and losers. And that's where things get tricky.
Schellbach asked his analyst team to examine their sectors, and the stocks within those industries, and consider five questions under a scenario of moderate AI adoption over the next three years.
■ What is the potential for the company to increase sales through the adoption of AI?
■To what extent can companies reduce costs via the adoption of AI?
■Will cost savings enhance margins, or will any margin uplift be competed away?
■Will AI allow the company to improve its competitive position?
■To what extent is the company likely to be threatened by the widespread adoption of AI through its industry and the wider economy?
The analysts then scored their sector and the companies they covered to arrive at an overall "AI opportunity" score.
Clearly, this is hardly scientific; the individual analyst's attitudes towards AI (are they a sceptic or believer?) can skew results, particularly at a sector level, and there is plenty of guesswork involved in individual scores.
Nonetheless, the analysts' scoring reveals some surprises.
At a sector level, tech-heavy sectors, including gaming, healthcare and information technology, scored highest, suggesting the biggest returns for AI adoption. Real estate, which is seen as both having limited room to adopt AI and a heightened threat from AI adoption (if, for example, the traditional office is further hollowed out by job cuts), posted the lowest score, just ahead of the transport and logistics sector.
But second on the list for big returns was the mining sector, where giants such as BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue have already seen solid gains from AI deployment in logistics, mine planning and production, and should see "consistent revenue upside and cost out opportunity stemming from AI adoption".
Inside each sector, Schellbach says, the cream rises to the top: the companies with the best AI opportunity scores are generally the biggest companies in the sector, with the deepest pockets, the best management teams, and entrenched competitive advantages. In the consumer staples sector, for example, Woolworths and Coles score highest, while in energy and utilities it's AGL and Origin on top.
Similarly, Macquarie Group and Commonwealth Bank scored best in the financial services sector, while in discretionary retail, Wesfarmers and JB Hi-Fi were judged to have the best chance of using AI to entrench their competitive dominance.
Indeed, the stocks identified by the UBS analysts as being most "AI ready" are beloved by investors as high-quality names. Schellbach says they generally trade at a 10-point price-to-earnings premium and 80 per cent relative return-on-equity premium versus the stocks judged as being "less favourably" exposed to AI. Does that mean potential AI success is already priced into these big names? No. The UBS analysts said AI opportunity had been priced into only six stocks: Commonwealth Bank, Macquarie Group, BHP, Rio Tinto, Technology One and Megaport.
On the other hand, the analysts name 11 stocks where they see good AI opportunities, but the companies are trading at discounts to sectoral peers.
These include utilities giant AGL, share registry group Computershare, retailers Endeavour Group and JB Hi-Fi, Qantas, insurer QBE, Rio Tinto, recycler Sims (which has a business that recycles computer chips), laboratory and radiology group Sonic Healthcare, logistics software group WiseTech and engineering giant Worley.
The UBS exercise is thought-provoking, and it will be fascinating to see how AI adoption actually rolls out on the ground. Three years is an eternity in the world of AI, but not long at all for an Aussie company investing in projects and deals that often take a decade to prove their worth.
But the project also highlights the challenge for Australian investors: it's tough identifying AI winners Down Under, compared to those in markets such as the United States or parts of Asia, where investors can buy the chipmakers, memory stocks, hyperscalers and AI model makers actually driving this revolution.
Schellbach says that may eventually be to Australia's advantage. When the heat around AI cools - and it eventually will - Australia's tech-lite exchange might just be a safe haven.
JAMES THOMSON
Fairfax Media Management Pty Limited
